title: Sales CRM for a real estate developer
lead: Designed an internal tool for a real estate developer’s sales team, covering everything from first contact and collecting client requirements to preparing offers and financial calculations.
meta: UX/UI design: product structure, user flows, interface design, responsive layouts and developer handoff
Sales managers, call center staff, brokers
Desktop and mobile: every key flow is designed for both
nda: Due to an NDA, this case uses anonymized descriptions and synthetic data. Real names, mockups, business data, internal documentation and client-specific logic are not published.

blocks.v: Outcome

v: Brought several work flows together into a single interface system where data, actions and deal stages are connected.
Made moving between stages of client work easier: the structure preserves context, reduces duplicate actions and lowers the risk of losing information.
Designed all key flows for desktop and mobile.

blocks.c: Desktop screens: client database, client profile, intake questionnaire, apartment selection, meeting schedule, calculations

blocks.v: About the project
The product is for teams that handle a high volume of inbound requests, client data, properties, meetings, calculations and deal materials.
The interface’s main job is to help managers guide a client step by step, without losing context between stages or manually re-assembling information across different tools.
The task
Design a multi-level panel that brings the key client-work scenarios into one service.

The focus wasn’t only on individual screens but on the product’s system logic: how users move between stages, where context lives, which data gets reused and how different sections support each other.

blocks.c: User flow: the client journey from first request to final offer

blocks.v: Functional areas
The service includes sections for:

v: working with the client database;
managing client profiles;
collecting and refining requirements;
working with properties and offers;
scheduling meetings;
preparing client materials;
running financial calculations;
configuring terms and programs.

blocks.c: Mobile versions of key flows: clients, questionnaire, apartment selection, mortgage calculator, final offer

blocks.v: The problem with the initial requirements
The original requirements listed features but didn’t fully explain how they should work together as one product.
During analysis I identified logical gaps between sections, unfinished scenarios, and places where users could lose context or have to repeat actions.
In essence, the job was to turn a set of separate functional blocks into a coherent system for working with clients step by step.

blocks.c: Meeting confirmation screen for the client

blocks.v: Process

v: Analyzed requirements and identified logical gaps between modules.
Proposed changes to the structure and user flows.
Designed key sections of the service around user roles.
Worked through interface states: empty states, errors, intermediate steps and return paths.
Mapped user flows for the main stages of client work.
Adapted interface solutions for desktop and mobile.
Prepared mockups and screen structure for developer handoff.

title: Financial dashboard for a real estate developer
lead: Designed an internal financial monitoring tool for a real estate development project, bringing planned and actual figures, periods, filters and data versions into one consistent interface.
meta: UX/UI design: section structure, dashboard and table logic, interactive prototypes, developer handoff
Finance specialists, department heads, management reporting users
Interactive prototypes shown at client meetings, then shared for internal testing
nda: Due to an NDA, this case uses anonymized descriptions and synthetic data. Real names, financial figures, internal data sources, mockups and client-specific logic are not published.

blocks.v: Outcome

v: Made financial metrics easier to analyze through a clear structure of dashboards, tables and comparison scenarios.
Delivered an interface that works both for detailed analysis and for presenting aggregated results to leadership.

blocks.c: Financial monitoring dashboard: revenue, expenses, share of advertising spend and monthly trends

blocks.v: About the project

I designed the financial monitoring section of a management panel for a real estate development project. The tool had to help the finance team work with a large set of metrics, compare planned and actual values, analyze variances and switch quickly between different data slices.
The interface’s main job was to make complex financial reporting clear, manageable and suitable for everyday use.

blocks.c: Sales table: plan vs. actual by project, variances and conversion rates

blocks.v: Key UX challenge: plan versions

In financial reporting, planned values can be updated, recalculated and used in different analysis scenarios. Users need to know which version of the plan they are comparing actuals against, and to switch between versions quickly.
I designed the version selection logic, the active-state display and the comparison scenarios so that this complexity stays manageable.

blocks.c: Table mode for working with planned figures

blocks.v: What mattered

v: Separate a quick overview from deep analysis.
Make the metric structure clear without overloading the screen.
Design filters, toggles and states for different comparison scenarios.
Present variances in a form that is easy to analyze.
Keep interaction patterns consistent across dashboards and tables.
Prepare the interface for large volumes of data.

blocks.c: Interactive prototype: switching data slices and comparing metrics

blocks.v: Prototype
I presented all work at client meetings as interactive prototypes, then shared the links so the team and the client’s staff could test them internally.

blocks.c: Prototype map: connections between screens and states
Early wireframes of the report structure

blocks.v: Process

v: Analyzed requirements and financial reporting workflows.
Structured metrics, slices, filters and comparison options.
Designed the logic of dashboards, tables and detail views.
Worked out scenarios for selecting planned data versions.
Built interactive prototypes to validate the interface logic.
Refined the screen structure based on team discussions.
Prepared mockups and interface states for developer handoff.

blocks.c: Dashboard block layout

title: Design system for a SaaS delivery platform
lead: Moved the client storefronts of a SaaS delivery platform onto a system of components and variables, and redesigned checkout to cut the number of steps needed to place an order.
meta: UX/UI design and design infrastructure: file structure, components, variables, client customization, checkout flows
SaaS for launching restaurant delivery: catalog, checkout, user account
nda: Due to an NDA, this case uses anonymized descriptions and synthetic data. Real names, mockups, client storefronts, internal documentation and product logic details are not published.

blocks.v: Outcome

v: Built a single design core that makes it faster to maintain different client versions of the product.
Simplified interface updates: new states, components and features no longer require rebuilding each mockup from scratch.
Redesigned checkout: fewer steps, with the key ordering actions gathered into a more direct and clearer flow.

blocks.c: Variable library: color, typography, sizing, spacing and element states

blocks.v: Starting point
Every restaurant on the platform gets its own client storefront: a menu catalog, a checkout flow and a user account. As the product grew, maintaining these storefronts became harder and harder.

v: mockups were scattered across different sections, which made the structure hard to navigate;
brand customization for each client required manual edits;
new features had to be repeated in several places;
keeping mockups up to date took more and more time as the number of storefronts grew.

blocks.v: The product was scaling, but the design infrastructure could no longer keep up.
Structure and design system
The first step was to organize the mockups. I grouped the interfaces around three key user areas: catalog and listings, checkout, and user account.
This separated the core product structure from client-specific details and made the file easier to navigate for design, management and development.
Variables and components
The design core included color variables, typography, sizing and spacing, base UI components, element states, and components for recurring screens and flows.

Components were bound to variables so that client customization no longer required rebuilding the interface by hand. This made it faster to adapt storefronts to different brands and to maintain product changes centrally.
System logic
The work went beyond visuals. It was important to think through how the design system would live in the real product:

v: which elements should be shared across all storefronts;
which parameters can change for a specific client;
how to update product flows without chaos in the mockups;
how to keep a consistent user experience across different visual settings.

blocks.v: Checkout redesign

was: a separate cart as an intermediate step;
re-entering data the system could already know.
now: cart, delivery details and main actions gathered in one flow;
some data pre-filled for signed-in users;
straight to payment with no extra steps.

blocks.v: Checkout became more direct: users see their order, check their details, confirm delivery options and go to payment without jumping between screens.
Impact

v: Maintaining mockups got easier thanks to a single design core, and client customization became faster and more predictable.
New components and states can be rolled out centrally.
Onboarding new clients got simpler through reusable components and variables.
Checkout became shorter and clearer for end users, and repeat orders more convenient.
The team’s focus shifted from manually rebuilding individual storefronts to developing the shared product core.

title: Website for a restaurant
lead: Designed a restaurant website with an unconventional two-part desktop layout, built around two key actions: ordering delivery and booking a table.
meta: Design and concept: visual direction, page structure, user focus, responsive versions, preparing mockups for the build
Brasserie 2.0, a restaurant from the team behind the Lambic chain
The site went live and was featured in a selection of the best websites built on Tilda

blocks.c: Two-part first screen: a fixed visual area with key actions on the left, scrolling content on the right

blocks.v: About the project

The new restaurant needed a website that would convey the atmosphere of the space before anyone set foot inside: through visuals, page structure, movement between content and constant access to key actions.

Unlike typical restaurant sites, where users scroll through blocks of menu, interior, contacts and forms one after another, this interface needed to be more expressive and memorable, without making development harder.
The task

v: create a site that stands out visually from typical restaurant websites;
convey the character and atmosphere of the place through the structure of the interface;
focus users on two main actions: ordering delivery and booking a table;
keep the responsive versions simple and cost-effective to build;
deliver a design that could be assembled quickly on Tilda without unnecessary technical complexity.

blocks.v: Concept

The core idea was built not around a decorative trick but around the page structure. On desktop the screen is split in two: the left side is a fixed visual area with a photo or video of the restaurant and always-available key actions; the right side scrolls, with text, descriptions and additional content.
This combines the emotional and the functional goals: users read about the restaurant while always seeing its visual identity, and can jump to booking or ordering at any moment.

blocks.c: How the two-part layout behaves on scroll

blocks.v: Why it works
Key actions never get lost while scrolling and stay available throughout the page, and the visual side isn’t a separate decorative block: it accompanies the content the whole way.
User focus stays within a simple two-part structure: the site looks unusual for the restaurant category but remains clear and easy to use.

blocks.c: Design concept: typography, photography and illustration

blocks.v: Responsive versions
The desktop structure made the responsive versions easier. Instead of designing several fundamentally different layouts for each screen size, the base structure adapted to different screens:

v: on tablet, one half of the desktop screen became the basis for a more compact layout;
on mobile, the content flowed into a sequential vertical layout;
key actions stayed visible and accessible.

blocks.c: Site screens and responsive versions

blocks.v: Process

v: Explored several options for the site’s visual and structural approach.
Developed the two-part desktop concept.
Planned the placement of the key actions: delivery and booking.
Built the structure of content blocks and visual accents.
Designed the responsive versions on a single underlying logic.
Prepared mockups for handoff to the Tilda build.

blocks.c: Three presentation concepts the final direction was chosen from

title: Website for a travel company in Irkutsk
lead: Redesigned the website of a tour operator running trips on the Circum-Baikal Railway: rebuilt the information architecture, created the design concept and more than 30 responsive layouts.
meta: Research and information architecture, prototyping, design concept, UI element library, responsive layouts
BAIKAL TRAIN, the official organizer of Circum-Baikal Railway tours since 2010, with more than 20,000 travelers a year
30+ responsive layouts for desktop and mobile

blocks.v: Outcome
Simplifying how content was organized and presented made it easier for users to explore the site and find information, and visual accents helped draw attention to the key elements.
The interface became stylish and clear, and the design concept reflected the company’s philosophy and positioning.

blocks.c: Home page: desktop and mobile versions

blocks.v: The task
The company asked for a refresh of its website: the design was outdated, the navigation needed simplifying and the content needed work.
Interviews and preparation

The work started with several client interviews to gather information and define requirements. They helped me understand the project’s overall problems and the client’s business goals, and frame the tasks the new design had to solve.
Research and information architecture
The interviews showed that the client had content problems: some texts were hard to read and didn’t match the target audience. This could get in the way of the users’ main action, booking a tour.

It also turned out that the navigation included several pages with very little content that could be merged into one section. I analyzed competitors and their design decisions, and together with the client we identified the strengths and weaknesses of existing solutions. This analysis became the basis for the new site structure.

blocks.c: Information architecture and user flows

blocks.v: Page design
At the design stage I prototyped the home page, defining its blocks and their importance to users. New pages were created and existing ones reworked on the same principle.

blocks.c: Home page prototype: blocks and their priority

blocks.v: Moodboard and design concept

The client wanted more visuals connected to nature and travel, so that the site would better reflect the brand. After studying similar sites and assembling a moodboard, it became clear that the client’s brand identity fit a “journey into nature” concept and matched the expectations of the niche.

blocks.c: Design concept moodboard

blocks.v: Page and responsive design
The home page set the overall color and type system. While designing the other pages I built a library of UI elements that kept growing, which sped up layout work and kept the design consistent.
Elements were designed for both dark and light themes, since the design used blocks of both.

blocks.c: Tour page
Inner pages of the site
Mobile versions: 30+ responsive layouts

title: Website and marketplace for a jewelry brand
lead: Restructured the website of the MIE jewelry brand and designed detailed mobile-first prototypes of every screen.
meta: Site restructure, detailed prototypes of all screens, an interactive prototype for the client presentation and handoff to the studio’s UI designer
MIE, a silver jewelry brand from Saint Petersburg with 20+ stores across the country, an online store and a marketplace presence
Mobile-first: most visitors come to the site from mobile devices

blocks.c: Mobile purchase flow

blocks.v: The problem
MIE had a website, but its complex structure made it hard to find jewelry quickly, which hurt conversion and therefore revenue. The design was also outdated and needed a refresh.
The task
My job was to rethink the site structure and design detailed prototypes of all its screens. The main goal of the new site was to increase the number of orders.
References

Before design began, the client shared their wishes and references for the expected result. I analyzed them and added my own ideas for each section of the site. Once the references were agreed, I moved on to designing the screens.
Design
Prototypes were developed scenario by scenario:

v: browsing a product and making a purchase;
signing up and managing the account;
finding products in the catalog with filters;
finding additional information that helps with the purchase decision.

blocks.v: Special attention went to mobile usability, since most of the traffic came from mobile devices. While working on the screens, I considered how best to implement features and arrange content for convenient use on both desktop and mobile.

blocks.c: Mobile screen prototypes: catalog, product page, checkout, account

blocks.v: Interactive prototype
The finished prototypes were made interactive: I set them up and prepared them for presenting to the client for approval and for handoff to the studio’s UI designer.
